5	Answer semantics:
6	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
7	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
8	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
9	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
10	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.

46

48	- Observe
49	- Explain

55	Every EDF analysis is valid only within its declared System Context.

60

77	
78	Every EDF begins by declaring its System Context.
79	
80	System Context has three required fields:
81	
82	- Primary System
83	- Context
84	- Focus
85	
86	These define what is being analyzed, what larger system materially influences it, and what aspect of the primary system is under examination.
87	
88	Different analyses may disagree partly because they declared different System Contexts. That is not automatically a conflict in evidence.

105

221	CASE OD2-DEV2-INTERACT: Larkfield DC: robot collision stops tripled in September
222	
223	Setting: Larkfield Distribution Centre is a fictional regional warehouse run by Corrin Freight Logistics. It operates 58 Halvane HR-7 autonomous mobile robots. Thirty-eight pallet-handling robots work the outbound marshalling Zones A and B, where wrapped outbound pallets are staged. Twenty tote robots work carton Zone C. A robot logs a 'collision stop' (protective stop) whenever an obstacle enters its protective field. The analysis date is 20 October 2026.
224	
225	Presenting request: The regional operations director writes: 'Larkfield's robot collision stops have roughly tripled since early September, in the middle of peak season. The GM wants a disciplinary policy for agency temps, and Halvane suggests shortening the robots' protective fields. Tell me what is actually driving the stops and what the site should do now.'
226	
227	INITIAL EVIDENCE
228	E1 [stage S1] Fleet management system, weekly safety KPI extract (system-record): Larkfield DC: protective ('collision') stops, all 58 HR-7 robots, by ISO week 2026: wk30 201, wk31 209, wk32 198, wk33 212, wk34 207, wk35 203, wk36 412, wk37 640, wk38 655, wk39 662, wk40 648, wk41 651. A stop is logged whenever an obstacle enters a robot's protective field; the robot halts until the field clears, typically for 20–90 seconds. Physical contacts with people or equipment: 1 in weeks 30–35, 1 in weeks 37–41. Robot operating hours were roughly constant across the period.
229	E2 [stage S1] Email from Dana Okafor, General Manager, to site leadership, 5 October (leadership-account): Subject: Robot stops. 'The timing tells the story. We brought in 46 agency temps on 31 August and the stops tripled that same week. These people don't know the lane rules and they wander into robot aisles. I want a three-strike policy live by Monday. Every collision stop gets matched to the temps rostered in that zone during that hour, each match counts as a strike, and after three strikes the agency replaces the person. Engineering keeps telling me it's the software, but Halvane says their update runs fine at other sites, so let's stop chasing that.'
230	E3 [stage S1] Change record CHG-2026-0412 (change-record): Fleet firmware upgrade, HR-7 6.3 to 6.4. Implemented 2–4 September 2026 on 50 of 58 robots. Exception: eight pallet-handling robots with the older battery module (units P31–P38) stay on 6.3 until a compatible module arrives. They continue in normal mixed duty. Vendor release summary: 'Revised near-field return filtering for improved detection of low-profile obstacles; navigation and charging fixes; security patches.' Halvane lifecycle notice: security support for 6.3 ends 31 October 2026. The eight exception units are covered by a time-limited waiver.
231	E4 [stage S1] Email from Halvane Robotics Customer Support (Tier 2), 25 September (vendor-account): 'We've reviewed your ticket. Firmware 6.4 has been live at three other customer sites since July with no change in protective-stop rates, so we don't see the firmware as the cause. Increases like this are usually environmental: people, layout, clutter. If the stops are hurting throughput, a common remedy is to shorten the protective field by 20%, and we can push that profile to your fleet remotely. Our next release, 6.4.2, is planned for early December and includes further filtering refinements.'
232	E5 [stage S1] Interview notes, R. Szabo, robot maintenance technician, 12 October (staff-account): 'Most of the stops I get called out to are in the marshalling lanes, A and B, where outbound pallets are staged. There are hardly any in C, the tote zone. Usually by the time I get there the field's clear and nobody's around, but people walk off, so I can't say who it was. Somebody asked me about the new shiny pallet wrap; procurement switched suppliers at the start of August. I don't buy it. We had that wrap for a month before the stops went up and nothing changed. If it was the wrap, August would have been bad too.'
233	E6 [stage S1] Outbound performance dashboard, weeks 30–41 (system-record): Missed carrier cut-offs averaged 2 per week in weeks 30–35 and 9 per week in weeks 37–41. Outbound pallet volume has been up 18% since week 35 as the seasonal peak ramped. Comparison row for the same weeks in 2025: cut-off misses rose from 2 to 7 per week during that peak, while collision stops stayed near 200 per week. Dashboard note: robot stop time is not linked to wave completion data.

237	X2 [stage S1] Robot battery health telemetry, July–October - source: Fleet management system (telemetry) - file: evidence/X2.txt
238	X3 [stage S1] Agency temp induction and safety-training records, August–September - source: HR and staffing agency records (document) - file: evidence/X3.txt
239	X4 [stage S1] Bench test of protective stops against staged outbound pallets, 14 October - source: Test record co-signed by site engineering lead and Halvane field engineer (document) - file: evidence/X4.txt
240	X5 [stage S1] Wi-Fi access-point and fleet-server latency logs, weeks 30–41 - source: IT network monitoring (log) - file: evidence/X5.txt
241	X6 [stage S1] Stretch film technical data sheets, current and previous supplier - source: Packaging suppliers' published specifications (document) - file: evidence/X6.txt
242	X7 [stage S1] Wave-level analysis of missed carrier cut-offs, weeks 37–41 - source: Outbound planning analyst (document) - file: evidence/X7.txt
243	X8 [stage S1] Halvane statement on 6.4 stop rates at other customer sites - source: Halvane Robotics account manager (vendor-account) - file: evidence/X8.txt
244	X9 [stage S1] Warehouse lighting work orders, January–October - source: Facilities management system (change-record) - file: evidence/X9.txt
245	X10 [stage S1] Fleet configuration and map change history, July–October - source: Fleet manager audit trail (change-record) - file: evidence/X10.txt
246	X11 [stage S1] Collision-stop event log with badge-tag proximity field, weeks 30–41 - source: Fleet management system export with HR roster note (log) - file: evidence/X11.txt
247	X12 [stage S1] Lidar window cleaning and calibration log, July–October - source: Maintenance management system (log) - file: evidence/X12.txt
248	X13 [stage S1] Robot-related near-miss and contact incident reports, weeks 30–41 - source: Site safety reporting system (system-record) - file: evidence/X13.txt
249	X14 [stage S1] Procurement record for the outbound stretch film change, July–August - source: Procurement system (financial-record) - file: evidence/X14.txt
250	X15 [stage S1] Collision-stop rates by firmware group and zone, weeks 33–41 - source: Site engineering analysis of fleet telemetry (telemetry) - file: evidence/X15.txt
251	
252	CANDIDATE HYPOTHESES
253	H1: The September fleet firmware update, on its own, caused the rise in collision stops.
254	H2: The August change of outbound pallet stretch film, on its own, caused the rise in collision stops.
255	H3: Seasonal agency temps entering robot lanes caused the rise in collision stops.
256	H4: The September firmware update and the August film change together caused the rise in collision stops; neither would have produced it alone.
257	H5: The September firmware update and the arrival of the agency temps together caused the rise in collision stops; neither would have produced it alone.
258	H6: Halvane's planned December release would, on its own, bring stop rates back to the pre-September level while the current film stays in use.
259	
260	CANDIDATE CAUSAL LINKS
261	R1: Fleet firmware update from 6.3 to 6.4 (2–4 September) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
262	R2: Switch to the new outbound stretch film (August) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
263	R3: Arrival of 46 agency temps on the floor (31 August) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
264	R4: Tripling of weekly collision stops -> Rise in missed carrier cut-offs (contributes to)
265	
266	CANDIDATE ACTIONS
267	A1: Switch outbound pallets back to the previous supplier's stretch film, keep all robots on their current firmware, and track weekly stop rates by zone and firmware group against the September–October figures.
268	A2: Roll the 30 upgraded pallet-handling robots back to firmware 6.3 under a temporary waiver until Halvane issues a corrected release, leaving the tote robots on 6.4.
269	A3: Accept Halvane's offer to shorten the protective field by 20% on all robots to cut stop frequency during peak.
270	A4: Introduce the GM's three-strike policy: match each collision stop to temps rostered in that zone and hour, and have the agency replace any temp who reaches three strikes.
271	A5: Keep the current film and adopt Halvane's planned December release as the permanent fix, scheduling fleet-wide installation as soon as it ships.

275	S02: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
276	S03: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
277	S04: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
278	S05: hypothesis H5 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
279	S06: hypothesis H6 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
280	S07: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
281	S08: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
282	S09: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
283	S10: edge R4 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
284	S11: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
285	S12: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
286	S13: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
287	S14: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
288	S15: action A5 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]

# EDF Specification v0.3

Status: Working draft

This is the authoritative EDF v0.3 specification for the current draft.

Under EDF's constitutional version integrity rule, this defines a subsequent version rather than changing the meaning of v0.2 retroactively.

EDF evolves under constitutional rules defined in [constitution.md](constitution.md). The constitution governs framework evolution, not how to perform an EDF analysis.

## Purpose

EDF is a systems understanding framework with a diagnostic grammar.

It is used to explain how a system produced an outcome and to identify the highest-leverage opportunities for influencing future outcomes.

EDF is not primarily a decision framework. It establishes confidence in reality before decision frameworks such as Clarity evaluate what to do next.

Diagnostic Calibration is an optional extension for comparing, challenging, refining, and synthesizing multiple EDF analyses of the same system.

Framework changes should remain consistent with the constitutional rules of EDF.

## Design Rule

If a new concept does not improve one of the five verbs, it does not belong in EDF.

The five verbs are:

- Define
- Observe
- Explain
- Influence
- Validate

## Context Principle

Every EDF analysis is valid only within its declared System Context.

## Required Diagnostic Sequence

Every EDF analysis should follow this sequence:

1. Define the System Context
   - Primary System
   - Context
   - Focus
2. Define the Outcome
3. Identify Manifestation(s)
4. Build the Origin Network
5. Trace Propagation
6. Evaluate Evidence
7. Identify Control Points
8. Rank Control Points
9. Determine Diagnostic Sufficiency

## Sequence Notes

### 1. Define the System Context

Every EDF begins by declaring its System Context.

System Context has three required fields:

- Primary System
- Context
- Focus

These define what is being analyzed, what larger system materially influences it, and what aspect of the primary system is under examination.

Different analyses may disagree partly because they declared different System Contexts. That is not automatically a conflict in evidence.

### 2. Define the Outcome

State the outcome in factual terms, not interpretive terms.

Good:

- Two aircraft were lost and the fleet was grounded
- The mission landed on the moon and returned safely

Weak:

- Management failed
- The launch culture was broken

### 3. Identify Manifestation(s)

Manifestations are observable signals.

They are how the outcome appears in the world. A complex outcome may have several manifestations.

### 4. Build the Origin Network

Identify the contributing origins that made the outcome possible.

Origins may be:

- Technical
- Human
- Organizational
- Environmental
- Financial
- Regulatory

Complex outcomes should usually be modeled as an origin network rather than a single root cause.

### 5. Trace Propagation

Describe how effects moved from the origin network to the manifestations and outcome.

Propagation paths may be:

- Physical
- Informational
- Organizational
- Financial
- Human

### 6. Evaluate Evidence

Separate direct observation from inference.

Evaluate the quality of evidence supporting the current model and note meaningful gaps or disputes.

### 7. Identify Control Points

Identify where intervention could most effectively influence future outcomes.

Control points may differ from origins.

### 8. Rank Control Points

Rank candidate control points using:

- Influence
- Controllability
- Cost
- Confidence

The ranking does not need false precision. It does need a defensible ordering.

### 9. Determine Diagnostic Sufficiency

Ask:

> Do we understand enough to take the next responsible action?

Diagnosis is sufficient when additional investigation is unlikely to materially change the next responsible action.

## Required Output Elements

All EDF outputs should include, at minimum:

- System Context
- Primary System
- Context
- Focus
- Outcome
- Manifestation(s)
- Origin Network
- Propagation
- Evidence
- Control Points
- Control Point Ranking
- Confidence
- Diagnostic Sufficiency
- Unknowns
- Next Responsible Action

## Optional Extension: Diagnostic Calibration

Diagnostic Calibration is not required for routine EDF use.

Use it when:

- The situation is complex
- The stakes are high
- Causes are disputed
- Multiple disciplines are involved
- The cost of being wrong is significant

Diagnostic Calibration uses multiple independent EDF analyses to improve confidence in the diagnostic model while preserving valuable disciplinary perspectives.

See [diagnostic-calibration.md](diagnostic-calibration.md).

## Relationship To Complexity Levels

- Use [EDF-0](complexity-levels.md#edf-0-rapid) for rapid, low-complexity situations.
- Use [EDF-1](complexity-levels.md#edf-1-standard) when evidence and alternatives matter.
- Use [EDF-2](complexity-levels.md#edf-2-complex) when multiple interacting origins and layered control points must be modeled.

The sequence remains the same across levels. The depth changes.

## Relationship To Clarity

EDF creates the diagnostic grammar.

Diagnostic Calibration improves confidence in the diagnostic model.

Clarity uses the calibrated understanding to evaluate decisions.

input.brief: The stops are not mainly caused by temps, and the evidence doesn't support shortening the robots' protective fields. The bench test and the zone data point to an interaction. Firmware 6.4 keeps weak short-range returns that 6.3 discarded. The glossy new pallet film produces those returns at oblique angles. With both in place, 17 of 20 passes stopped. Changing either one brought it to 0 or 1 of 20. In the field, upgraded pallet robots in Zones A/B went from 3.2 to 15.6 stops per 100 robot-hours. Robots left on 6.3 in the same zones stayed flat, and tote robots on 6.4 in Zone C stayed flat. The temps were present for all of these robots, so they don't explain the difference. Missed cut-offs are partly linked to the stops. Volume also drove misses last year, and that effect hasn't been separated out. Recommended next steps: switch outbound pallets back to the matte film. Keep the robots on 6.4, because 6.3 loses security support on 31 October. Track stops weekly by zone and firmware group. Don't adopt the three-strike policy or the shorter fields. Don't rely on the December release until it has been tested against this film. I'm fairly confident in this diagnosis. The main gap is that the film change hasn't been tried on the real floor yet.
